title: Andy Burnham promises more devolution and public control of essential services
description: Andy Burnham has promised to set out plans for "stronger public control" of essential services as he addressed the House of Commons for the first time
body: Andy Burnham has promised to set out plans for "stronger public control" of essential services as he addressed the House of Commons for the first time since taking power. The prime minister said "a series of wrong turns" since the 1980s had seen economic power in the UK privatised and pointed to the water industry as "a leaking monument to that approach - a country run in the private rather than public interest".  He reiterated his belief that political power had been centralised and announced he would be making devolution powers available to more areas in England. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused Burnham of offering "more government control, more taxes and more politicians"."His diagnosis is completely wrong, his theory of growth is completely wrong, he thinks that if government spends more money, we will all get richer - that is not how this works," she said. Badenoch also warned the prime minister that his new job would be "very different" to his previous Greater Manchester mayoral role where he "did not have to make difficult trade-offs".  Burnham became prime minister on 20 July shortly after Parliament closed for the summer recess. Tuesday marked the first day of the new parliamentary session and provided his first opportunity to address MPs and take questions. He told the House of Commons that "Britain is not where we would wish it to be", but promised to "build a new sense of optimism around the country".Following his 10 years away from Parliament, Burnham said he was returning with a "clear diagnosis" of what had gone wrong in the country. "From the 1980s, this country took a series of wrong turns," he said. "Political power was centralised, economic power privatised, the country deindustrialised, austerity followed, hollowing out councils and depriving them of the agency to act to reverse any of this."And then Brexit compounded the damage, ushering in a decade of low growth and stalled regeneration."In the months before becoming prime minister, Burnham stopped short of calling for full nationalisation but said he wanted to see greater public control of water and energy.On Tuesday, he promised that a plan to achieve this would be produced "later in the year". Pressed on his plans for the water sector by Conservative MP Alison Griffiths, Burnham said it was important to "look at all possible solutions"."It's a very regrettable situation that the privatisation of water has left us in a position where we're going to find it very difficult to reverse," he added. Burnham said his time as Greater Manchester mayor had given him "a clear theory of growth", namely that devolving powers to regions outside London would boost their economy. He argued the approach had worked in Manchester and now he wanted "every single place across our regions and nations to be able to do the same, creating the conditions for good growth in every postcode".Some MPs have raised concern that areas without mayors - and the new powers that have come with them - would suffer, leading to a two-tier system. Efforts to secure a devolution deal in Cornwall have been stymied by the county's reluctance to form a group with Devon but also to having a mayor. Burnham appeared to have accepted the county's concerns, telling the House of Commons his government would work with Cornwall Council and its six MPs on a devolution deal "with or without an elected mayor".He added that he would be extending "the same offer to all parts of England without devolved power".He also said he was interested in exploring "a local model of devolution" in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Shortly before Burnham's speech to Parliament, Sir Keir Starmer said in a surprise announcement that he would be stepping down as an MP, less than two months after he quit as prime minister. Burnham began his speech by paying tribute to his predecessor telling the House of Commons that Sir Keir had "given this country a lifetime of public service" and created a "platform to change this country for the better". In his wide-ranging statement, which lasted three-and-half-hours, Burnham gave an indication of his approach on several other issues including welfare.He suggested that providing more council homes and thereby bringing down rent for more people would be the "Labour way" of reducing the benefits bill.The prime minister also committed to introducing legislation that would allow homeowners to move more easily from the leasehold system to a commonhold form of ownership.Asked by Badenoch about defence spending, Burnham said he had specifically chosen John Healey to be his chancellor because of his "commitment to defence". Healey resigned as defence secretary earlier this year, accusing then-prime minister Sir Keir of failing to commit the resources needed to keep the country safe. Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey used his question to argue that too much power in the UK was in "the wrong hands" and called for "fundamental change" of the political system.Burnham said he would look at the voting system but would not introduce any changes before the next general election. Both Reform UK's Richard Tice and the Green Party's Ellie Chowns asked whether the government would approve new drilling licences at the Rosebank oil field and the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea. Tice urged the PM to allow more drilling saying it was "madness to import gas from overseas when we have our own gas in the North Sea" while Chowns opposed such a move arguing that the "climate damage they would create hugely outweighs any possible benefit". Burnham promised to take a "pragmatic approach" and said he wanted the transition to renewable energy to be done "as effectively and affordably as possible".

schema.headline: Andy Burnham promises more devolution and public control of essential services

title: Keir Starmer announces he is standing down as MP
description: Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer has announced he is to stand down as an MP to focus on a role in international affairs.The move will trigger a
body: Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer has announced he is to stand down as an MP to focus on a role in international affairs.The move will trigger a by-election in the London seat of Holborn and St Pancras, long a Labour stronghold, which he has represented since 2015.Sir Keir, who left Downing Street in July, had previously said he would stay on as an MP until the next UK general election, which is not due until 2029.But in a surprise statement hours before his successor Andy Burnham made his debut in the House of Commons, he said he was resigning to work on issues such as international affairs and violence against women and girls.Paying tribute to his predecessor, Burnham highlighted Sir Keir's work with Ukraine and the Hillsborough Law drawn up under his government to improve the accountability of public officials, which is going through Parliament."He has given this country a lifetime of public service, particularly for those fighting for justice," he added. "His leadership took our party from one of its worst defeats to its best victories and created a platform to change this country for the better. We will use it well, and we wish his family the very best for the future."Announcing his resignation, Sir Keir told the Camden New Journal, external it had been a "huge honour and privilege" to represent the London constituency for 11 years, ending weeks of speculation about whether he would remain an MP.He added he was ready to "pass the baton to a successor", telling the newspaper it was the "right time" for him to leave Parliament.He said: "I will now focus on other things and that will be international affairs including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast-changing world."I will also continue, as I have done for a long time now with others, to work on combating violence against women and girls; that is an issue that matters to me hugely. "It's work I started before I became an MP and it's work I'm keen to continue after I'm an MP. So international affairs on the one hand, and continuing my work on violence against women and girls on the other."Sir Keir became prime minister after winning a landslide majority at the 2024 election, but quit No 10 after pressure from Labour MPs to stand aside.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch wished Sir Keir the best for the future adding: "I can understand why he would not want to spend time with the Labour MPs who treated him so badly after he won them their seats."Tory Party chairman Kevin Hollinrake accused Sir Keir of making "another U-turn having pledged to stay on", prompting a "costly by-election for taxpayers".A date will not be set for the by-election until Sir Keir formally resigns his Commons seat. This will only be confirmed once the government has given him a crown appointment, the mechanism that disqualifies him from being an MP.Labour expects to select a candidate for the by-election by 9 September, according to the party's website.Holborn and St Pancras has long been a Labour stronghold, with Sir Keir securing a more than 11,000-vote majority at the last general election in 2024.Labour's main challenger in the seat is likely to be the Greens, who came second by vote totals at this year's local elections in wards that make up the constituency - with 29.8% of the vote to Labour's 39.5%.Reform UK came a distant third by these vote totals, and the Greens' share was higher if they are given the votes in two wards where they stood aside.Candidates for the by-election will not be confirmed until a later stage, but the Greens hinted that leader Zack Polanski was considering a run at the seat.A spokesperson for the party said Polanksi, currently a member of the London Assembly, had "always made it clear he would like to be a London MP".

schema.headline: Keir Starmer announces he is standing down as MP

title: Remarkable US oil deal puzzles analysts - and angers many Venezuelans
description: From the moment elite US troops swooped into Nicolás Maduro's compound in Caracas to forcibly remove him from power in January, President Donald Trump
body: From the moment elite US troops swooped into Nicolás Maduro's compound in Caracas to forcibly remove him from power in January, President Donald Trump made clear that securing control over Venezuela's oil resources was a key goal of his administration.The United States would "run" Venezuela, he said at the time, and manage the sale of Venezuelan oil for the foreseeable future.The signing of a huge US-Venezuela oil deal in Caracas on Wednesday marked the fruition of that plan. The agreement grants a US-led company 100-year concessions over 17 oilfields in Venezuela, amounting to a staggering 65 billion barrels of crude. That equates to more than a fifth of the country's proven oil reserves.Beyond the eye-watering numbers, both sides heralded the deal as good for their respective nations. President Trump called it "the biggest oil deal in world history", while the interim Venezuelan President, Delcy Rodríguez, said the agreement was "historic", and would generate $100bn (£74bn) in investment and more than $200bn in tax revenue.Others profoundly disagreed."This is a terrible deal. [Rodríguez] has given away 20% of the national patrimony for nothing," said Trump's former special representative on Venezuela and Iran, Elliott Abrams. "I think she is simply complying with the demands she's getting from Washington."On Tuesday, the White House released a fact sheet which set out some details of the deal's framework. The US government will work alongside a private business in Venezuela called North American Blue Energy Partners (Nabep), the second largest private oil producer in Venezuela after Chevron.One extraordinary detail of how the Trump administration will work with Nabep is that the US government will have "veto power over the appointment of any member of the board of directors, and a majority of Nabep's board of directors must be US citizens".With the ongoing US war with Iran increasing prices at the petrol pumps, a boost in oil production outside of the Middle East could affect consumers. Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum told Fox Business the pact was "shifting the geopolitical centre of the global energy markets" away from what he called the "choke points in the Middle East" and back to the Western Hemisphere.There is a logic to the US-Venezuela partnership, Elliott Abrams argued, while Gulf oil supplies are currently so unreliable. But he said the terms are so one-sided they are a "kind of fever dream of what colonialism looks like".The White House has spoken of the deal having "re-established the Monroe Doctrine", an 18th Century principle exerting US power across South America - "purging foreign malign influence from our backyard and ensuring American dominance in our hemisphere is never again questioned".Despite the insistence from both governments that the plan will benefit both Venezuelans and Americans, it is not without pitfalls and clear unanswered questions.The proposed timeframe alone is problematic. Trump has said the agreement will generate profit within two or three years. Energy experts, however, warn the dire state of the Venezuelan oil sector means a decade is more realistic.Luis Pacheco, of the Baker Institute at Rice University in Houston, told BBC Mundo that Venezuela needs to invest about $100bn over eight years in order to return to its oil production levels of 30 years ago."It's important to know who will manage those resources and for what purpose," Pacheco said. "Are they going to put the same people in charge of managing that money who already squandered the biggest oil boom of the century?" he asked, referring to past mismanagement of the country's oil wealth.The Venezuelan opposition is concerned the deal deepens President Trump's relationship with Delcy Rodríguez, whom they accuse of heading the same regime as Maduro. The Trump administration not only decried Maduro's government as a corrupt drug cartel, but surrounded Venezuela with the biggest armada of the modern era.The ease and speed with which Washington has now pivoted to working with Maduro's former vice-president infuriates the opposition.The Nobel Peace Prize winner and presidential hopeful, María Corina Machado, may choose not to publicly criticise President Trump, whose support she needs if she hopes to come to power. Others, though, have been more forthcoming."You chose to use the power of the United States not to liberate Venezuelans, but to ally yourself with our oppressors," said Venezuelan economist, Ricardo Hausmann, on social media, directing his comments at the US Secretary of State Marco Rubio."You opted to push through an asset seizure, an unconstitutional agreement with an illegitimate and oppressive government, instead of using the leadership of the United States to first restore constitutional order and democracy," he said.The lack of an imminent election in Venezuela – or, indeed, any clear plan towards one – strikes many opponents as a betrayal.There is betrayal felt at the other end of the ideological spectrum, too. Although the governing socialist party, PSUV, has backed Rodríguez over the US deal, many Venezuelan socialists see it as capitulation.After almost three decades opposing Washington's influence in the region, they feel she has gifted the country's most valuable asset to the old enemy.The deal "hands over [the oil] and opens the doors to a new colonialism of the United States," said Rafael Ramírez, who served as the head of the state-run energy firm, PDVSA, and as the oil minister under former President Hugo Chávez.In early 2008, Chávez presented his Sunday television programme, Aló Presidente, from former ExxonMobil oilfields in the Orinoco River Belt. Having expropriated some of the oil company's assets in the region, he was in a defiant mood."We have the reins in our hands and we won't ever let them go again," he said of the state-run oil company's ownership of oilfields, and denounced how previous Washington-friendly governments had turned Venezuela into "a nation of gringos"."It was a theft of our nation but the Bolivarian Revolution has put a stop to it," he thundered to applause from PDVSA employees.Yet it was one of his disciples – his handpicked successor's successor – who has now signed this opaque deal with Washington and praised it as a victory for Venezuela.

schema.headline: Remarkable US oil deal puzzles analysts - and angers many Venezuelans

title: Jurors in Lindsay Clancy trial deadlocked but  judge asks them to keep trying
description: Jurors in the trial of Lindsay Clancy are deadlocked after four days of deliberations, but a judge has asked them to keep trying.Clancy, a resident of
body: Jurors in the trial of Lindsay Clancy are deadlocked after four days of deliberations, but a judge has asked them to keep trying.Clancy, a resident of Massachusetts, is facing murder charges for killing her three children at their family home in 2023.Her lawyer does not dispute that the 36-year-old former nurse killed the children, but argues that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time and was unable to distinguish right from wrong.After discussing the case for several more hours on Tuesday,  jurors were sent home for the day and asked to return in the morning."I just want to thank you for all your hard work and commitment so far in this case," the judge told jurors before sending them home.The Massachusetts mother is charged with three counts of first-degree murder, as the prosecution argues she made a calculated, intentional decision to kill them. The jury, made up of nine women and three men, began deliberating last week after hearing weeks of testimony from dozens of witnesses. On Tuesday, audible gasps could be heard in the courtroom as Judge William Sullivan read out a note from the jury indicating that it was deadlocked. Clancy, who was left paralysed after jumping from a second-floor window shortly after the killings, appeared stoic as she sat in a wheelchair beside her lawyer.Clancy is accused of strangling her kids - Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, who was eight months - with fitness bands in their Massachusetts home  in January 2023. The defence argues that Clancy was experiencing postpartum psychosis, a severe mental health condition that can develop after childbirth, and that she should therefore not be held criminally responsible for the killings.If found guilty of first-degree murder, the intentional and premeditated killing of another person, Clancy will face a mandatory life sentence in prison without the possibility of parole.She could also be found guilty of a lesser charge, including second-degree murder - committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without prior planning - or manslaughter - unintentionally killing "by wanton and reckless conduct". In either of those instances, she would face time behind bars.If she is found not guilty by reason of insanity, she will not be set free - she would instead be sent to a psychiatric hospital where her status would be periodically reviewed.  She could stay in hospital for the rest of her life.

schema.headline: Jurors in Lindsay Clancy trial deadlocked but  judge asks them to keep trying

title: Sexual assaults in Ceuta happening almost every day, prosecutors say
description: Spanish prosecutors say 23 sexual assaults, including nine against children, have been recorded in Ceuta since the mass influx of migrants into the Sp
body: Spanish prosecutors say 23 sexual assaults, including nine against children, have been recorded in Ceuta since the mass influx of migrants into the Spanish exclave  at the end of July.That number meant there was almost one case every day, Ceuta's chief prosecutor Silvia Rojas said.She told El País newspaper migrant girls were "particularly vulnerable because of their irregular status in the territory".At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July and although most have returned, as many as 5,000 remain - leading to unrest in the autonomous city in North Africa and a crisis for Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.Between 1,400 and 1,600 of the estimated 5,000 migrants still in Ceuta are children, according to Rojas.Among the suspected attackers are four Moroccans, three Spaniards and a Belgian, Efe news agency reports.There have been scenes of violence in recent days as tensions flare up between migrants and local residents. Sánchez called the second meeting of his national security council in a week on Tuesday to tackle the issue.Rojas said the influx had led to an exponential increase in sexual assault, and many victims did not file a report, either out of fear of because of their "current situation in Ceuta". The Spanish Society of Epidemiology said the border crisis had highlighted the difficulty in detecting and tackling violence against migrant women and girls.One 24-year-old woman from Morocco told the BBC she had "put her life in danger" by travelling to Ceuta, and described being sexually assaulted while sleeping among a group of men and women. "I was shocked… If I had known this, I wouldn't have come."Emergency doctor Susana Ascaso said last month her department at Ceuta University Hospital had treated several sexual assault victims, including one who was just 10 years old.Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo said a multi-million euro aid package had been approved by the cabinet that would help provide essential services and cover care for unaccompanied children.The territory's conservative mayor, Juan Jesús Vivas, has called on Spaniards to take part in demonstrations across mainland Spain in support of Ceuta on Wednesday, which coincides with the city's annual holiday.The Spanish government is facing bitter criticism from its opponents for its handling of the crisis. The hard-right Vox party said Sánchez had not "lost control of Ceuta - he has handed it over".Arantxa Campos, president of the Ceuta Employers' Confederation, told the BBC: "We can't do anything unless these people leave. "We don't have a plan from the government. We don't have anything. We don't even know when they're going to finish screening everyone."The prime minister said on Monday that King Felipe VI would visit Ceuta "as soon as conditions allow", seen as an attempt to assert Spanish authority over the exclave. Morocco has a long-standing claim over Ceuta and its fellow autonomous city of Melilla. The last time a Spanish head of state visited the territories in 2007, Rabat pulled its ambassador from Madrid, and another royal visit may cause further diplomatic tensions.In an interview with Spanish radio channel Cadena Ser, Sánchez made a point of saying the king had not visited Ceuta for 20 years - even though Felipe has only been on the throne for 12 years and it was Juan Carlos who visited in 2007. He also asserted he was the only prime minister to have made an official visit to Ceuta while in office, having travelled there on 31 July as the crisis took hold. Some Spanish commentators noted that his remarks appeared to criticise the king, whom he then met later in the day.Unlike his political opponents, Sánchez has been careful to avoid blaming Morocco for stoking the surge of migrants. He said on Monday that no intelligence reports pointed to "any involvement in one way or another" from the Moroccan authorities.Instead he focused on disinformation on social media "associated with both Russia and Israel and an international far-right movement that always uses migration, not only to attack Spain but also Europe". He told Cadena Ser it did not mean "it must come from a state actor" and appeared to indicate the crisis had been stoked after the influx. Government spokeswoman Elma Saiz later confirmed his allegation, saying there was evidence that "various digital forums amplified what happened with the intention of fracturing and polarising Europe".Russia and Israel have both denied any involvement. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar accused the Spanish prime minister of "a blatant lie" and Russia's foreign ministry spokeswoman demanded proof to support Sánchez's allegations.A large number of social media posts appeared in August portraying the border fence between Morocco and Ceuta as safe and easy, even though at least 100 people died while trying to swim around the border fence, according to figures from the mayor.Spanish fact-checking website Maldita said before 30 July, when the influx began, messages circulated on Moroccan social media encouraging people to attempt the crossing, after a June ruling by Spain's Supreme Court.The opposition People's Party (PP) has criticised Sánchez for "exonerating" Morocco and pointing the finger in other directions. Borja Sémper, a spokesperson for the party, said tens of thousands of people could not have moved towards the Ceuta border without Morocco's knowledge.Morocco has denied orchestrating or being involved in the mass crossing.

schema.headline: Sexual assaults in Ceuta happening almost every day, prosecutors say

title: Spaces in male prisons in England and Wales fall to lowest level of year, sources say
description: The number of available spaces across the male prison estate in England and Wales has fallen to its lowest this year, sources have told the BBC.As of
body: The number of available spaces across the male prison estate in England and Wales has fallen to its lowest this year, sources have told the BBC.As of 1 September, there were about 1,500 free spaces,  just under half the number available at the start of June, which Ministry of Justice (MoJ) figures put at 3,040.It comes as Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced changes to the government's early release scheme, which will mean more prisoners, including those convicted of manslaughter, will remain behind bars for longer. Justice Secretary Alex Norris told the Commons on Tuesday the scheme, which was launched to reduce prison overcrowding, is needed to maintain confidence in British justice.An investment of £110m, which will come from existing budgets, will be used to convert unused office space, laundry rooms and storage space into cells, the MoJ said.Speaking in the Commons on Tuesday, the justice secretary told MPs the government's plan to free up capacity in the UK's male prison estate will ensure the justice system "commands the confidence of the British public""This is the right thing to do, and I pay tribute to his wife Lissie and mother Debbie (Adlam), who campaigned for this," he said. "We would like to have gone further, but due to the lack of investment in the previous government's 14 years, we are unable to do so."He added Labour has been forced to take "tough decisions" because it had inherited a justice system "on the brink of failure".Norris also told MPs the government plans to "bring forward legislation" to end Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) sentences "once and for all – by the end of this Parliament".IPPS sentences were used where prisoners were considered to pose a significant risk of causing serious harm to the public. Once they had served a minimum term they could only be released if the Parole Board was satisfied they no longer posed a risk to the public.Shadow Justice Secretary Nick Timothy called plans to end IPP sentences a  "fag packet policy".He said: "This is the Government's fifth early release policy in just six weeks since the prime minister took office."At every stage, we were told ministers had no choice but to include dangerous criminals, because the alternative would be the collapse of the entire system."Now the plan is to stop one group of dangerous criminals leaving prison early by letting a different group of dangerous criminals out instead."Earlier, Norris told the BBC prisoners being released early did not mean "freedom" and victims would have a say in restrictions placed on those criminals.Asked where clothes would be washed if laundry rooms were converted into cells, Norris told BBC Breakfast: "Of course we're going to make sure that the prisons can still function properly."This is a creative look, as I say, around our estate and being able to use some space that we can re-prioritise."Norris said he suspected the number of extra prison spaces created from freeing up existing space within prisons would be "landing somewhere in the middle" of 200 and 900.But the chairman of the Prison Officers' Association, Mark Fairhurst, said: "You can create as much additional space as you like, and build as many new prisons as you like, but where are the staff coming from to supervise people? Nobody wants to be a prison officer anymore."Prisons in England and Wales are running at 97% capacity.Under the early release scheme some 4,500 prisoners are now expected to start being let out of prison in tranches from October.On Sunday, the prime minister told BBC Breakfast anyone convicted of manslaughter would be excluded from the scheme, following a campaign from PC Andrew Harper's family to block the release of two men convicted over his killing in 2019.Extra prison space would also be created by deporting more foreign prisoners and releasing some inmates serving indefinite sentences.Government figures show there were 10,134 foreign nationals held in custody on 30 June, 3,283 of whom were on remand and would not be eligible for deportation.In the year to June, 5,962 foreign offenders were sent back to their home countries - the highest rate of deportations since 2017 and a 12% increase on the previous year.

schema.headline: Spaces in male prisons in England and Wales fall to lowest level of year, sources say

title: Ariana Grande ends tour and steps back from public life
description: Ariana Grande made an emotional exit on Tuesday night, as she wrapped up her Eternal Sunshine tour, and prepared to step back from public life.The sin
body: Ariana Grande made an emotional exit on Tuesday night, as she wrapped up her Eternal Sunshine tour, and prepared to step back from public life.The singer was occasionally close to tears - most notably during One Last Time, the song that took on extra meaning as an anthem for survivors of the 2017 Manchester terror attack."London, I'm going to need you to help me on this one," she said, kneeling down to be near the audience throughout the performance.Last month, Grande announced a break from all future public-facing appearances following months of intense speculation about her health and appearance.The step-back includes Grande's withdrawal from a production of Stephen Sondheim's Sunday in the Park with George at London's Barbican next summer.She was due to appear alongside her Wicked co-star Jonathan Bailey. He also pulled out of the production on Tuesday.On stage in London, Grande showed no signs of fragility or poor health - other than a foot injury that required her to swap her trademark stilettos for a succession of knee-high platform boots.Nonetheless, she sprang across the stage in sync with her dancers, often on tip-toe to compensate for the lost height of her high heels.But her composure slipped during the song Nowhere, Nobody, as she sang the line: "Hard to believe in a perfect ending."The blip was short-lived, though. Professional to the core, Grande was never less than magnetic on stage.Even before that announcement, Grande had described the Eternal Sunshine tour - which started in the US in June - as "one last hurrah", saying she wanted to take more acting roles after her Oscar-nominated performance in Wicked.That meant her 10 show residency at London's O2 Arena represented many fans' last chance to see her in concert. They flew in from all over the world - from China and Australia and cities all across Europe - with 200,000 people attending the London dates alone. On the second night, Grande surprised the audience by bringing out her Wicked co-star Cynthia Erivo for a rendition of their movie duet For Good.Across the board, reviews were positive."There's no question about it - Ariana Grande is one of the best singers of her generation," wrote Rolling Stone magazine, external, noting that "there were no signs" of the singer "struggling or not wanting to be there".The Telegraph called the show "flawless", external, praising its "Hollywood-indebted" staging, and Grande's "genuine affection for Britain".The BBC's review highlighted quieter songs like Imperfect For You, describing them as "delicate and gorgeous and strangely intimate in a room of 20,000 people".But Guardian writer Kate Solomon said she was "gripped by genuine concern", external for Grande, even when she was enjoying the show, adding: "I really hope this tour does not go down in history for the wrong reasons".The NME, by contrast, was left breathless by the star's physical prowess."Throughout the show," marvelled Nick Levine, external, "she skips across the stage in skyscraper heels that most drag performers would baulk at."That wasn't the case on the final night, however, due to what Grande described as a "deep cut" on her foot.Writing on Instagram, she assured fans the injury wasn't serious, insisting she was "on the mend" and would complete her final shows "even if I am a few inches shorter than usual".She did so with a huge smile spread across her face, leaning into the big notes of Dangerous Woman, and sprinting across the stage during Break Free - one of many up-tempo highlights.She ended the show as she always does - attached to a harness, ascending into the rafters of the O2 and disappearing.Fans were left wondering when, if ever, they'd see her perform again.

schema.headline: Ariana Grande ends tour and steps back from public life

title: How the conviction of Duane Davis could help inspire efforts to find the killer of the Notorious B.I.G.
description: Wallace, a New Yorker, was once one of Shakur's friends, but the two became rivals and embodied the East Coast-West Coast feud that dominated 1990s hi
body: Wallace, a New Yorker, was once one of Shakur's friends, but the two became rivals and embodied the East Coast-West Coast feud that dominated 1990s hip-hop.  Wallace was killed in Los Angeles a few months after Shakur and in similar circumstances - a drive-by shooting. No one has ever been charged."Tupac's murder and Biggie's murder are two of the great cultural touchstones of our lives," said Justin Tinsley, a journalist for ESPN's Andscape and the author of "It Was All a Dream: Biggie and the World That Made Him." "Those two men, they were so unique, talented, and impactful, separately," Tinsley told the BBC. "But it's impossible to tell each of their stories without telling the other's.""When you talk about these cases, they're always going to be connected because there are so many mutual figures involved with them, and ancillary figures," he said.Theorists have long believed the two murders were linked. Wallace's name came up during Duane Davis' trial. He and Davis were at the same party the night Wallace was killed, and police interviewed Davis about it.The investigator who conducted that interview even testified at the Tupac murder trial.The breakthrough in finally solving the Shakur case largely came down to one thing: Davis' own words. Through documentaries with the media, his own memoir, podcasts and even a secret police interview, he acknowledged his role in Shakur's death. Davis said he tossed a firearm in the backseat and his nephew, Orlando Anderson, used the gun to fatally shoot Shakur as they pulled up alongside his vehicle in Las Vegas on 7 September, 1996.Anderson was shot dead in 1998, having denied killing Shakur.During the trial, there were no eye-witnesses to place Davis as being in the car, no murder weapon presented, no video or photo evidence. His defence team went as far as to argue there wasn't even proof that he was in Las Vegas that night.Rahmani said it was a difficult case to prosecute. He noted the rumours and speculation surrounding Davis were nothing new and had been around for decades - but the decision to charge him and go to trial was an "uphill climb" - a gutsy move - for prosecutors. "Look, when you're a prosecutor, you're expected to win every time. They made a difficult decision to charge a case that a lot of people thought might be a loser," he explained. "And they got justice, where other people didn't even bother trying." Davis' attorney Michael Sanft asked the jury to consider "what facts do you have?" He urged the panel, before they decided their guilty verdict, to discredit his client as a liar who told tales to sell books and make money. "There's no proof," he argued to the jury. The moment the guilty verdict was read in court, there was an outpouring of emotion among Shakur's family. Some cried and wiped tears with tissues. Others hugged and held hands. A family member embraced one of the prosecutors in the case. At a press conference on Tuesday, Clark County District Attorney Steve Wolfson thanked the judge, prosecutors and Shakur's family members, who he said were very relieved and "finally have justice.""Their loved one was murdered," he said. "They waited 30 years for a trial. It's very understandable that they were relieved."Trial lawyer attorney Shaun Kent said the case really evolved with each interview and moment that Davis decided to talk about the case."There are no other witnesses, besides him," Kent told the BBC before the trial, noting that the "strongest witness against him, is him".Rahmani believed Davis likely would have never faced charges if he had stayed silent. "He really couldn't stop himself," Rahmani added. "Even when he was arrested and in custody, he was giving interviews." Much of the Shakur trial forced the jury to place themselves back in the 1990s, at a time of intense gang violence that had infiltrated roots into hip-hop music and rivalries between East-Coast and West-Coast rappers.It was a time of deep-rooted mistrust in policing and a street code that forbade reporting to authorities. Even Shakur, after being hit multiple times in the drive-by shooting that would later kill him, refused to talk to authorities. "We'll take care of it," he said in an ambulance as an officer tried to question him.The silence was echoed months later in the shooting death of Biggie Smalls. Biggie, one of the biggest East Coast rappers, was leaving an after-party in Los Angeles for the Soul Train Music Awards, when a black Chevrolet pulled up to his vehicle at a red light and opened fire on 9 March, 1997. It was almost exactly six months after the shooting that killed Shakur, one of the biggest West Coast rappers.Both were Grammy-nominated artists at the top of their genre, making millions and receiving constant radio play. Their feud spilled over into their lyrics, and also led to threats and physical violence. Violence erupted on the streets of Los Angeles following both shootings, as street gangs sought to hold one another accountable for the rappers' deaths.For years, neither murder led to arrests or convictions, just rumours and conspiracies. "People will search for closure in any way they can get it," Tinsley said. "People are trying to make sense of it for 30 years."Like Shakur's death, countless theories and names have surrounded the death of Biggie in Los Angeles, but the Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) have not made any arrests."It's really a stain on the LAPD. The fact that this could happen and not a single arrest was made and no one was prosecuted," Rahmani said, noting Biggie's killing happened on a public street in the middle of the second most populous US city. "Prosecutors don't like to lose," Rahmani explained. "But, maybe this [Tupac's conviction] will embolden folks in Los Angeles to maybe take another look at it, a cold case that's coming up on 30 years." Asked about the cases and whether the Tupac murder conviction could revive Biggie's death, the LAPD told the BBC that it was aware of the conviction and the investigation into Biggie's case remained active. "The murder of Christopher Wallace remains an open, unsolved case within LAPD's Robbery-Homicide Division," Lt Elpidio Orozco said, urging anyone with any tips to call authorities. Though Wallace's case has gone cold, the public's interest has not."They've been gone longer than they've been alive," Tinsley said, "But the enduring mythology around these guys and their deaths will always be a topic of conversation."Kayla Epstein contributed to this report.

schema.headline: How the conviction of Duane Davis could help inspire efforts to find the killer of the Notorious B.I.G.

title: Premier League clubs set new transfer spending record
description: This summer, 38% of deals involving a transfer fee have been from one Premier League club to another, which is an increase from last year, when the fi
body: This summer, 38% of deals involving a transfer fee have been from one Premier League club to another, which is an increase from last year, when the figure was 30%. That then increases to 48% in instances where Premier League clubs have bought players from lower down the English football pyramid.On top of that, the Premier League net spend remains over £1bn for this window - by far the most in Europe - despite many of the biggest sales this summer coming from the English league too. Bundesliga and Ligue 1 clubs have received more in transfer fees than they have spent.Aside from French-based duo Barcola and Bouaddi, the majority of major signings made by Premier League clubs this month have been from rival clubs in the same division.They include England team-mates Rogers and Anderson, while Newcastle sold Tonali to Spurs and Guimaraes to Arsenal. Manchester United snapped up Baleba from Brighton after a 12-month chase to aid their midfield revamp, while Tottenham's recruitment of Fernandes and Savio is in the same category.But why are English clubs buying each other's players more than ever this summer instead of shopping abroad for the biggest deals?One reason could be the temptation for players who are proven in the Premier League.Many of last season's big-money signings - with a good chunk of them coming from the Bundesliga - failed to meet expectations or justify their transfer fee.There have also been deals this summer involving the same clubs, possibly with accounting in mind, with Chelsea and Villa selling players to each other.And there is also a feeling that teams abroad increase the transfer fees they are asking for when English teams - with all their TV riches - show interest in their players.

schema.headline: Premier League clubs set new transfer spending record

title: Wincobank baby death: Newborn died of stab wounds - police
description: A newborn baby girl who was discovered fatally injured at a house in Sheffield died as a result of stab wounds, police have said.The baby was found at
body: A newborn baby girl who was discovered fatally injured at a house in Sheffield died as a result of stab wounds, police have said.The baby was found at a house on Holywell Heights in the Wincobank area on Sunday morning, after police were called to reports of concern for her safety.South Yorkshire Police said despite the best efforts of police and paramedics, the baby died at the scene. Seven people aged between 15 and 37 were arrested on suspicion of her murder. Two of them, aged 26 and 37, were later bailed, but police confirmed on Tuesday a warrant had been obtained to extend time in custody for the remaining five as inquiries continued.Det Ch Insp Tom Woodward, leading the investigation, said: "We recognise this is deeply distressing for those who would have loved to have a chance to love this baby girl, for the emergency services who responded and for the community who will inevitably be shocked by this incident."Everyone involved in responding to this tragedy - from the first officers and paramedics on the scene to the detectives now leading the investigation - has felt the profound impact of this investigation."He added: "Our commitment to this little girl is unwavering. We will confront every difficult and distressing challenge and pursue every line of inquiry with determination and care to secure justice for her."We know the local community will hold her in their thoughts and support us as we work through this complex investigation."A South Yorkshire Police spokesperson said officers were continuing their investigations in the Holywell Heights area and asked anyone with information that might be useful to contact them.

title: 'I've never been to Afghanistan': Six million deportees forced to start over under the Taliban
description: Figure caption, Watch: BBC's Lyse Doucet reports on the biggest cross-border movement of peopleByLyse DoucetChief international correspondentReporting
body: Figure caption, Watch: BBC's Lyse Doucet reports on the biggest cross-border movement of peopleByLyse DoucetChief international correspondentReporting fromTorkham crossing and KabulThe elderly grimace, hobbling on crutches, and wide-eyed children stare, cradling chickens carried from homes they were forced to leave behind."It feels good to be in my own country," 35-year-old Nazia says, just minutes after she crosses from Pakistan, where she was born, into Afghanistan.The Torkham crossing, known as "Zero Point", is where one hard life ends and another begins."But I've never been to Afghanistan before and many people here don't even have enough bread to eat," Nazia sighs as she heads, two of her children in tow, toward registration counters festooned with white and black Taliban flags.Nearly her entire family, eight sisters and their offspring, were deported to Afghanistan this year from Pakistan or Iran.They are part of the biggest cross-border movement of people anywhere in the world.Millions of Afghans have fled across the borders to Pakistan and Iran for decades – seeking refuge or employment - and the number escaping Afghanistan has continued to rise since the Taliban takeover in August 2021.Most are now being forced to return as these two neighbours crack down on undocumented migrants. Nazia and her family were undocumented but the UN and human rights groups say the security sweep is reaching far beyond that group to include registered Afghans too. Even Pakistan now publicly says that Afghans with Proof of Registration cards are not exempt.The expulsions show no sign of stopping. Image source, AFPImage caption, Trucks carrying returnees parked along the highway near the border The number forced to return this year from Pakistan and Iran has already reached another million, according to the UN's Refugee Agency, the UNHCR."In a little under three years, we've seen six million people, a population that is itself the size of a small country, come back to Afghanistan," observes Charlie Goodlake, spokesperson for the UNHCR in Afghanistan."We've never seen in recent history a return movement on this scale," he underlines, standing in the baking heat in the tented village close to the border.It's a desolate landscape of tarpaulin and plastic shelters, many now tattered and torn, erected by the UN and other aid agencies to provide refuge for a few nights for a people arriving with nowhere to go.Many returnees have not set foot in Afghanistan for decades; many like Nazia have never been here at all."I left 45 years ago during the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and most of my brothers were born in Pakistan," explains Sarwar, who arrived a few days earlier with seven brothers and their families in a convoy of 40 people and the jumble of their worldly goods packed into a lumbering Pakistani lorry."We spent a long time there, so of course I felt heartbroken when they forced us out of our home," he says. "But, despite all that pain, I am also happy because I am finally free of harassment by Pakistan's police."Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Afghan returnees deported from Pakistan arriving at the Torkham crossing Every family we met told us they had experienced prejudice and harassment by authorities in Pakistan.The Pakistan government has not responded to the BBC's questions, but a foreign ministry spokesman told a briefing in Islamabad on Sunday that "the Government of Pakistan undertakes the necessary measures to prevent any instance of harassment or maltreatment of Afghan nationals in Pakistan. If such incidents have taken place, they are sporadic and are dealt with fully in accordance with the law". Both Pakistan and Iran say it's past time for Afghans to go home, accusing some of posing a security risk, and others of being a financial burden.The expulsions from Pakistan and alleged abuse intensified after a major escalation in fighting between Pakistan and Afghanistan last October. In February, Human Rights Watch highlighted "door-to-door raids, late-night home searches and arrests without warrants".In Iran, which claimed last year to host more than four million undocumented Afghans, the mass deportations were accelerated after its 12-day war with Israel and the US in June 2025.The New York based Centre for Human Rights in Iran accused the authorities of using the post-war climate to "cast suspicion on Afghan migrants - accusing them of espionage and branding them as potential spies for Israel".The UN's refugee agency continues to underscore the humanitarian principle that any return should be "voluntary, safe and dignified".But in Torkham, Sarwar's sister-in-law Zarina laments the precarious future they face: "We have no resources to start a business or earn a living, and we don't even own a tent to live in".Image caption, Zarina, 40, is among the million Afghan who have returned this year alone Inside the barren transit tent, which provides little escape from scorching 41C heat, Zarina sits alongside an anxious huddle of women and their children. Are they worried about the future for women and girls in a country where the Taliban has barred women from much of public life, including secondary school and university?Forty-year-old Zarina turns to make a sweeping gesture with her arm: "Look at them, they're all girls. Of course I'm worried."Some returnees are not just worried; they're terrified."I don't leave this house," a former Afghan security guard, first deported from Iran and then Pakistan, nervously tells us when we meet him far from the border in what he hopes is a safe house. "We are all living in fear including my wife and children who are also afraid to go outside."He dismisses the Taliban government's amnesty, announced days after their return to power which declared that former government officials, security personnel and civil servants would not face retaliation and were encouraged to return to work."I have no trust in their amnesty because many of my colleagues have been killed." He says his case had been registered with the UN but was deported before he could be transferred to a safer country. Financial hardship magnifies the pain. The steep cuts in foreign aid worldwide are especially sharp in Afghanistan where the Taliban are still stuck in sanctions linked to terrorism and human rights.Pakistan confirmed on Sunday that 16,000 vulnerable Afghans have now been granted, on humanitarian grounds, a temporary exemption from being deported – a decision welcomed by the UN.  But sources estimate that the number of Afghans in Pakistan at risk of serious harm, including women and girls who would be denied education, could be as high as 250,000.Image caption, Zarina says she is worried about the future of the girls who cannot attend secondary school and university in Taliban-run AfghanistanAt the graceful foreign ministry compound in Kabul, Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi tries to put on a brave face."There's no doubt that we need some help," he admits. "There is pressure due to their return but in the long run, it will benefit them as well as Afghanistan."In the first years after the Taliban swept to power in 2021, some of their ministers made light of humanitarian issues, saying God would provide. The UN now estimates that 21.9 million people, nearly half the country, need assistance this year to survive. The UN's children agency, UNICEF, said last week that one million children faced "life-threatening" malnutrition."No country in the world could handle this kind of crisis on its own," UNHCR spokesperson Goodlake assesses, while acknowledging Taliban government efforts to help returnees as they arrive.But, he adds, "We also know that many of the restrictions and edicts they put in place, particularly on women and girls, don't help us elicit international support".Muttaqi reiterates his government's line that matters like girl's education are "internal issues" for Afghans to resolve.The severe restrictions on the lives of girls and women is one of the major issues in the Taliban's international relationships and that has cost them. Five years on, only one country, Russia, has formally recognised their rule.But when asked about this, Muttaqi points to the deepening diplomatic and economic ties with neighbours such as China and India, as well as Central Asian states. As for Kabul's relative isolation from western nations, he asks, "those who didn't have relationships with us over the past five years, what have they achieved?"He answers his own question: "Nothing."We heard that word - "nothing" - from every family we met at Zero Point, but in a much different sense. All were embarking on the hardest of homecomings, beginning all over again - with almost nothing.

schema.headline: 'I've never been to Afghanistan': Six million deportees forced to start over under the Taliban

title: Cleveland Police get extra £2m after spate of crimes follows A66 crash
description: Fatal crash police get £2m to tackle serious crimeImage source, Cleveland PoliceImage caption, PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough were killed in the
body: Fatal crash police get £2m to tackle serious crimeImage source, Cleveland PoliceImage caption, PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough were killed in the crash on the A66 near MiddlesbroughByFederica BedendoNorth East and CumbriaUpdated 1 hour agoA police force is being given an extra £2m after a spate of crimes followed the death of two police officers and five men in a head-on crash, the home secretary has announced.Shabana Mahmood pledged the funding after Prime Minister Andy Burnham paid tribute to the officers killed, and in light of the challenges faced by Cleveland Police following the seven deaths on the A66 near Middlesbrough on 22 August.PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough died when a Volkswagen Passat going the wrong way on the A66 at South Bank hit their vehicle. The five men in the Volkswagen also died.The force has since arrested 27 people for activities linked to "serious and organised crime".About 200 police officers from outside Cleveland Police have been drafted in to help the force tackle organised crime following the crash.In the days following the deaths, police dealt with a series of incidents including homes being rammed and vehicles set on fire at a vigil.Mahmood said "lawlessness of any kind" would "never be tolerated"."In light of the situation the force has faced, we will allocate an additional £2m to Cleveland Police to tackle serious crime in the area," she said.She paid tribute to the two officers who died in the A66 crash and said she recognised how "unnerving" the current climate would be for the "law abiding citizens" in the community.She said: "We will do our best to support the Middlesbrough community, which is hurting and grieving right now, and we hear the call from the members of this house representing it for a discussion about investment in policing and police numbers."'Not a solution'Conservative MP Chris Philp told Mahmood the extra £2m pledged was "wholly inadequate" and said he was concerned about a shortfall in funding for the force in general.He said: "This lawless gang chaos should never have been allowed to take root in the first place."Commenting following the announcement, Cleveland's Labour Police and Crime Commissioner (PCC) Matt Storey said a "one-off payment" was "not a solution".He said: "It does nothing to address the chronic underfunding that has disadvantaged policing in Cleveland for years."He called on the government to act to address "deep-rooted funding inequalities"."Cleveland Police needs at least an additional £20m every year to recruit and retain 200 more police officers, to strengthen efforts to crack down on serious and organised crime."Speaking in the Commons, Mahmood said she was committed to reviewing the funding formula, which is used to determine the funding that each force is given.She added the previous government had taken away 20,000 police officers from forces nationally.Image source, Owen Humphreys/PAImage caption, Seven people, including two police officers, died in the wrong-way crash on the A66 on 22 AugustThe Labour MP for Middlesbrough and Thornaby East, Andy McDonald, told Mahmood that Cleveland Police had the highest rate of crime for any police force in England and Wales.He said the latest figures showed about 123 recorded crimes per 1,000 residents, yet the force had received the "largest percentage reduction" in officers since 2010."Police numbers are not the only factor, but a force facing the highest demand in the country needs the resources to respond," he said.He added the £2m would address some of the extra funding needed but he wanted to discuss how funding shortfalls could "urgently and permanently be corrected".Mahmood said she would be happy to meet with MPs in the area to discuss the issue and wider funding concerns.Luke Myer, Labour MP for Middlesbrough South and East Cleveland, also called for the government to review how funding was assigned.Mahmood said "reviewing and reforming" the formula was "absolutely critical" and said she would be updating MPs on a schedule for changes to be discussed, once an independent review on police force structures had been completed.Follow BBC Tees on X,, external Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external and listen to Radio Tees on BBC Sounds. title: Iliman Ndiaye: Manchester City sign winger from Everton for £65m
description: Iliman Ndiaye's journey to Manchester City has been something of a scenic route after he completed a move to Etihad Stadium from Everton in a deal wor
body: Iliman Ndiaye's journey to Manchester City has been something of a scenic route after he completed a move to Etihad Stadium from Everton in a deal worth up to £65m. The deadline day move for the Senegal winger, 26, is worth £60m plus a further £5m in add-ons - a little over six years since he made his professional debut playing in the seventh tier of English football."I've worked my whole life for an opportunity like this," said Ndiaye, who has signed a five-year contract with the club. "City are one of the best clubs in the world and I've seen them win everything as I've grown up. To be able to write my own chapter in a story that special is the chance of a lifetime and I'm determined to grab it with both hands." Ndiaye had held talks with Saudi Pro League side Al-Hilal earlier in the summer while Tottenham had agreed terms with Everton on Friday night for Ndiaye, when it looked as though Richarlison would move the other way in a separate transfer.However, sources indicated Richarlison failed to agree personal terms with his former club and as a result, Spurs were unable to proceed with the Ndiaye transfer.The move comes on the same day City agreed to pay a joint-British transfer record fee of £125m for Chelsea midfielder Enzo Fernandez.The Argentian international is set to become City's eighth summer arrival with Enzo Maresca's side having also signed Elliot Anderson, Geronimo Rulli, Ayyoub Bouaddi, Allan Elias, Jeremy Monga and Pierce Charles. As a 19-year-old living in London, Ndiaye was in the youth ranks of Boreham Wood and playing Sunday league football when he was invited for a one-week trial with Sheffield United.Two trial games were enough for the then-Premier League club to sign the talented teenager, although it would be another 18 months until he made an appearance for the Blades.Instead, he spent the second half of the 2019-20 campaign on loan at Hyde United in the Northern Premier Division, six levels below the top division. He made six appearances in his very first taste of professional football, often risking missing the last train back to Sheffield to stay out on the training pitch."It's not always been easy in my career," said Ndiaye.  "But I always had the belief that I could play for a team challenging for the biggest prizes and now I'm here." After returning to Bramall Lane, Ndiaye made his Premier League debut in March 2021 against Leicester City but it would be another three-and-a-half years until he became established at the highest level following the Blades' relegation.Two seasons in the Championship culminated in Ndiaye spearheading their return to the top flight in 2023 with 14 goals in 43 starts but he was then sold to Marseille that summer.Ndiaye struggled during a season in France before joining Everton for an initial £16m fee in July 2024.A firm fan favourite on Merseyside, "Skiliman" scored 15 goals and provided four assists in 67 Premier League games for the Toffees before his City move. Everton fans may also point to recent moves in the Premier League involving City, such as the sale of Savio to Tottenham for an initial £75m, as further evidence that the club should have demanded more for Ndiaye.On the other hand, Everton are effectively quadrupling the initial £16m they paid Marseille to sign Ndiaye two years ago for a player whose underlying numbers, at this stage at least, are not truly elite.In the Premier League last season, Ndiaye only ranked joint third at Everton alone for goal contributions (nine), with Beto (10) and Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall (12) providing more. It is reasonable to assume that those numbers for Ndiaye will improve in a more attacking team at City but his general creativity is also middling as things stand.He created 36 chances in total in the Premier League last season, ranking him only fourth at Everton. Toffees midfielder James Garner created 26 more. Jack Grealish, whose season ended in January because of injury, created eight more.Grealish has effectively replaced Ndiaye at Everton following his loan move from Enzo Maresca's side. Casting the net a little wider, 45 Premier League players have recorded more goal contributions than Ndiaye's 19 since he made his Everton debut two years ago.As a 26-year-old set to be surrounded by better players, it would be no surprise should his numbers flourish at the Etihad.But even in today's money, £65m for Ndiaye's current output may not be as questionable a deal as it sounds.

schema.headline: Iliman Ndiaye: Manchester City sign winger from Everton for £65m

title: Israel warns it will retaliate if UK imposes sanctions
description: Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar has warned his country will retaliate if the UK imposes sanctions against it over the potential expansion of set
body: Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar has warned his country will retaliate if the UK imposes sanctions against it over the potential expansion of settlements in the West Bank.  Addressing Parliament for the first time as foreign secretary, Ed Miliband said he would introduce a "comprehensive reset" of policy on Israel "in the coming weeks". He said the government would examine how to stop UK companies "financing, constructing or advertising new settlements" in the occupied West Bank.Responding, Gideon Saar told Hebrew-language news website Ynet: "If Britain acts against Israel, Israel will act against Britain."  "If they act, I think they will be making a big mistake," he said.Last month, Israel opened up tenders for the construction of some 1,200 settlement homes in the so-called E1 area - a strategically important area east of Jerusalem. The plans have drawn widespread international condemnation.The development would in effect divide the West Bank in two and isolate East Jerusalem. Miliband said the plans are "illegal under international law" and called them "the crossing of a red line, as it cuts through the heart of the West Bank and risks making a Palestinian state unviable".UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham also warned that Israel's statement about the E1 area could "imperil or end" the two-state solution in the Middle East.All settlements are illegal under international law and, under global pressure, Israel held off for decades on plans to build in the area.

schema.headline: Israel warns it will retaliate if UK imposes sanctions
